opus-5.5.text:
I think the convergence comes from the fact that both teams are ultimately being shaped by the same constraint, which is the data. On the surface they started from quite different places. Physical Intelligence came in with a very strong vision-language-action framing: take a pretrained VLM, inherit all that semantic knowledge from the internet, and then teach it to output actions. Generalist leaned much harder into the scaling side of the story, collecting enormous amounts of real-world manipulation data, thinking about throughput of data collection almost as an engineering problem in itself, and treating the model more like a foundation model trained from physical interaction.

But once you actually try to make a robot do dexterous, long-horizon tasks reliably, you run into the same walls. Internet knowledge helps with understanding the instruction, recognizing objects, some common sense, but it doesn't tell you how much force to apply when folding a shirt or how to recover when a box slips. That knowledge only comes from embodied data. So the VLM-first approach inevitably has to invest heavily in large-scale robot data. And on the other side, if you only scale robot data, you quickly realize you want the model to generalize to new instructions, new objects, new scenes, and that's exactly where pretrained vision-language representations give you leverage. So the data-first approach inevitably pulls in more pretrained knowledge and language conditioning.

Architecturally you also see them meet in the middle. Both end up with some kind of large backbone for perception and reasoning, plus a component that produces continuous, high-frequency actions, whether you call it an action expert, flow matching, diffusion head, or action chunking. Both care about cross-embodiment training, both care about post-training on specific tasks, and both are starting to think about reinforcement learning from real deployment to push reliability from, say, 80% to 99%.

So my view is that the difference was more in emphasis and starting point than in the destination. The underlying physics of the problem is the same: you need semantic generalization and you need physical competence, and the only way to get both today is a large pretrained model plus a lot of high-quality interaction data plus some form of self-improvement. Whoever starts from one end gets pulled toward the other. In that sense, the convergence isn't really a coincidence, it's almost a sign that the field is discovering what the right recipe looks like. The real differentiation in the next few years probably won't be the model philosophy, but who can build the most efficient data flywheel and get robots deployed in the real world earliest.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization to new instructions, objects, and scenes, but does not identify broad initial household-task competence and learning an unfamiliar task after one demonstration as complementary requirements.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they converge because, in the end, both are answering the same question: where does the data come from, and what do you do with it once you have it.

On the surface they look very different. Physical Intelligence started very much from the "foundation model" mindset. Build a big vision-language-action model, pre-train on as much robot data as you can gather across many embodiments, and bet that scale plus diversity gives you generalization, the same way it did for language. Generalist came at it from the other side. They were obsessed with the data engine itself, with collecting enormous amounts of real manipulation data through hand-held devices and human demonstration, with the argument that the bottleneck isn't the architecture, it's that robotics simply never had an internet-scale corpus.

But if you look at what each company actually had to do over the past two years, they walked toward each other. Physical Intelligence discovered quite quickly that scraping together heterogeneous datasets wasn't enough, that the quality and coverage of data matters enormously, and so they had to build their own collection operation, their own teleoperation fleet, their own data curation pipeline. Meanwhile, Generalist found that once you have hundreds of thousands of hours of demonstrations, you can't just train a small policy on it. You need a large model with strong pre-training, with language grounding, with the ability to transfer across tasks, otherwise all that data is wasted. So they ended up building a foundation model too.

That's the first reason for convergence: the problem forces it. Data without a model that can absorb it is useless, and a model without the right data is a toy. Any serious team eventually has to own both halves.

The second reason, I think, is more fundamental and it's about the nature of the physical world. In language, you can pretend that the model is the product. In robotics, you can't. The robot has to actually succeed in a kitchen or a warehouse, and success rate is unforgiving. Whatever philosophy you start with, the feedback loop from deployment pulls you toward the same practices: post-training on task-specific data, some form of reinforcement learning or self-improvement from the robot's own experience, careful attention to failure recovery, and a very tight coupling between hardware and the learning system. These are not stylistic choices. They are what the physics demands.

And the third thing is talent and ideas flow. These are small communities. People move between labs, papers come out every week, and the good ideas, whether it's flow-matching action heads, or chunked action prediction, or using human video as pre-training, get adopted by everyone within months. So the architectural differences shrink very fast.

Where I think they may still differ is not in the method but in the business bet. Who do you collect data for, which tasks you prioritize, whether you sell a brain to hardware companies or build the whole stack. That's where the real divergence will be. But the technical recipe? I think in three years you'll look at both and struggle to tell them apart, because they will both be large multimodal models trained on massive real-world manipulation data and refined through deployment. Same destination, different front doors.

r001.rationale: The response discusses data, models, and deployment as reasons the companies’ approaches converge, but it does not identify broad initial task competence and one-shot learning of unfamiliar tasks as complementary requirements for household robots.

astra-6.text:
I think they converge because they’re trying to solve the same underlying problem: how to turn diverse robot experience into a policy that generalizes beyond the situations it was trained on.

You can come at that by emphasizing the data collection system, or by emphasizing the model and the learning algorithm. But those choices become coupled. A stronger model needs broader, more informative data, and a larger dataset only becomes useful if the model can learn the structure shared across tasks and environments.

So I’d expect convergence at the level of the overall system: collect experience, train a general policy, deploy it, discover where it fails, and use those failures to guide the next round of learning. That doesn’t mean their architectures or products will become identical. It means that, ultimately, both have to make that same learning loop work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalizing across training situations and a repeated data–train–deploy loop, but it does not identify broad initial household-task competence or the ability to learn an unfamiliar task after being taught once as complementary requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they converge because they’re trying to solve the same underlying problem: how do you turn diverse robot experience into a policy that generalizes to new tasks and environments?

You can start from different places—put more emphasis on collecting data, or put more emphasis on the model—but those choices become coupled. The model determines what data is useful, and the data reveals what the model is missing. Eventually, you need a loop where you collect experience, train a policy, deploy it, identify failures, and collect more targeted experience.

And in robotics, the physical world is the test. A model has to translate what it sees into actions that actually work. So I’d expect convergence in the overall recipe: broad data, a general-purpose policy, and continual improvement through deployment. That doesn’t mean their architectures or products become identical. It means the requirements of the problem push them toward similar systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broad data and policies that generalize to new tasks, but does not identify both broad initial household task competence and learning an unfamiliar task after one teaching as complementary requirements.
